subject: Tenant screening — the 5 criteria that actually predict outcomes
preheader: Rent-to-income · prior-landlord reference · credit · employment · eviction history · 3 you can skip

marketSnapshot.headline: Tenant screening — the 5 criteria that predict outcomes
marketSnapshot.body: The single decision that has the biggest impact on whether a rental property performs to plan: who you put in it. Five screening criteria actually predict outcomes statistically. Three commonly-used criteria don't (and screening on them is a fair-housing violation). New landlords usually under-invest in screening and end up with the loudest, most-aggressive applicant. Experienced ones use a consistent process and end up with measurably better tenants.

stats.label: Avg cost of one bad tenant

dealSpotter.address: Example: A-class property · high screening volume
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 80-120 applications · screen first qualified, not first applied
dealSpotter.body: A-class property in a desirable city neighborhood. The wrong screening process here means you end up with the loudest, most aggressive applicant rather than the best one. The right process: list at market, require online application + credit + verification documents within 72 hours, screen in the order received. Aim for 30%+ rent-to-income, 670+ FICO minimum, no eviction history. Disqualify quickly so you don't burn time on weak candidates.

dealSpotter.address: Example: B-class property · vet inherited tenants carefully
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Existing tenants · ALL their history matters
dealSpotter.body: Property currently occupied. The under-asked-about due diligence: get the rent rolls for the LAST 24 months (not just current), the security deposit ledger, and any communication-with-tenant log. Tenant who's been there 8 years paying significantly below market isn't 'great long-term tenant' — they're locked-in below market with no path to market without disruption. The math on assuming below-market tenants vs vacating to relist is real and worth modeling before bidding.

dealSpotter.address: Example: C-class property · screening market is soft
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 60-90 day lease-up timeline · budget the vacancy honestly
dealSpotter.body: C-class property in a market with softer rental demand. Budget 60-90 day lease-up timeline for first-rental properties unless you're at A-class. That's $3,500-5,500 of vacancy that doesn't show up in the listing's pro-forma 5% vacancy assumption. Pencil it in honestly. The biggest source of 'this deal didn't pencil like I thought' is unrealistic vacancy assumptions at the C-class level.

blogFeature.title: Property management yes or no — the actual math
blogFeature.excerpt: Good PMs run rigorous screening that catches issues a single landlord wouldn't spot. The fee they charge often pays for itself on screening alone — bad tenants cost 3-12 months of lost rent plus damages.

qa.question: What 5 things actually predict whether a tenant will be a good tenant?
qa.answer: (1) Rent-to-income ratio. Solid threshold: rent should be ≤33% of verified gross monthly income. Below 30% is great; above 40% predicts late payments and stress. Verify via 2 most-recent pay stubs OR employer letter (not just self-reported). (2) Prior-landlord references — specifically the second-to-last landlord, not the current one (current ones often give glowing reviews to get the tenant out). Ask: did they pay on time, did they take care of the property, would you re-rent to them? (3) Credit score. 670+ is the typical investor threshold. Below 620 has 2-3x the eviction risk. Above 720 is great. (4) Employment stability — at the current employer for 12+ months is a positive signal. Frequent job changes correlate with payment risk. (5) Eviction history — any prior eviction filing (even dismissed) raises future-eviction risk substantially. Three things that DON'T meaningfully predict outcomes: presence of pets, marital status, having children. Screening on those is also a fair-housing violation. Stay disciplined on the five that matter.
